tool.name: EstimatedShortestPath

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/geometric-tools/estimated-shortest-path.html
Orders a set of points into a short travel route -- a survey route you can load straight into a GPS. Three route types: a simple shortest path (the route starts and ends at whichever two input points give the shortest total), a round trip from a single start/end point (for example, where you left the truck), or a route from a fixed start point to a fixed end point. Legs are straight lines between locations, not road-network routes. Outputs the route polyline and an optional copy of the points numbered in visit order.

tool.usage:
You have generated your sample locations -- now you have to go stand on every one of them. This tool answers the field question that follows every sampling design: in what order should I visit these points so I spend my day surveying instead of walking? It pairs naturally with every point generator in this add-in -- the Random Point Generator, the Random Sample Array Generator, Repeating Shapes, and the Spatially Balanced Sample (GRTS) -- but any point feature class works, and a layer's selection is honored.
Three route types. The first, Simple Shortest Path, finds the shortest open path through all the points, starting and ending at whichever two points give the shortest total -- use it when you just want the points ordered efficiently and do not care where the route begins. Start and End at Same Point makes a round trip: give a single point (for example, where you left the truck) and the route leaves it, visits every point, and returns to it. Start and End at Different Specified Points runs from a fixed start point to a fixed end point -- a trailhead to a pickup spot. The start/end features can each be a single-point feature class or one selected point on a larger layer.
Straight lines, not roads. The legs are straight lines between locations (computed in an automatic equal-area projection for latitude-longitude data, with the total reported as true geodesic length). This is NOT a road-network route -- Esri's Route and Network Analyst tools do that, and they need a network dataset to do it. A straight-line route is exactly what cross-country fieldwork wants, and the visit ORDER it finds is usually an excellent visiting order even when you drive between points.
"Estimated." Finding the truly shortest route through many points is the classic traveling-salesperson problem, and exact answers are computationally out of reach beyond a few dozen points. This tool uses a careful heuristic -- nearest-neighbor and cheapest-insertion constructions polished by 2-opt and Or-opt refinement -- that in testing lands on the true optimum for small problems and typically within a few percent of it for large ones. More powerful methods exist: the celebrated variable-depth search of Lin and Kernighan (1973) and its descendants can edge within about a percent of the optimum, but they are famously delicate to implement correctly, and a subtly wrong route solver fails silently. This tool deliberately stays with the simpler, verifiable move family -- the same trade Babin, Deneault, and Laporte (2007) recommend for practical use. The same inputs always produce the same route. Around a thousand points solve in about a second; the practical ceiling is roughly 8,000 points.
The outputs. The route polyline carries Route_Type, N_Stops, Length_km, and Length_mi. Ask for the optional points numbered in visit order and you also get a copy of your points with Visit_Order (1, 2, 3, ...), Src_FID (the source point's Object ID), and Leg_km (the length of the leg leaving each stop) -- label the points by Visit_Order and the map reads like an itinerary. For ModelBuilder, the tool also returns the number of stops and the route length in kilometers as derived outputs.
Advanced: extra randomized solver attempts re-run the polish from shuffled starting orders and keep the best result -- occasionally a touch shorter, proportionally slower. The default (3) is a good balance.

param.displayname: Points to visit (a layer's selection is honored)

dialogReference.para: The points to route through -- typically sample locations from the Random Point Generator, Random Sample Array Generator, Repeating Shapes, or Spatially Balanced Sample (GRTS) tools, but any point feature class or layer works. A selection is honored; multipoints are exploded.

Simple Shortest Path: the shortest open path through all the points, starting and ending at whichever two points give the shortest total. Start and End at Same Point: a round trip from a single point you supply (for example, where you left the truck). Start and End at Different Specified Points: from a fixed start point to a fixed end point.

param.name: loop_point
param.displayname: Start/end point (a single point, or a single selected point)

dialogReference.para: Round trips only: the point the route leaves from and returns to -- for example, where you left the truck. Supply a feature class holding a single point, or select exactly one point on a larger layer.

param.name: start_point
param.displayname: Start point (a single point, or a single selected point)

dialogReference.para: Fixed start/end routes only: where the route begins. A single-point feature class, or one selected point on a larger layer.

param.displayname: End point (a single point, or a single selected point)

dialogReference.para: Fixed start/end routes only: where the route ends. A single-point feature class, or one selected point on a larger layer.
The route, as one polyline visiting every point: Route_Type, N_Stops, Length_km, Length_mi (the length is true geodesic). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

param.displayname: Output points numbered in visit order (optional)

dialogReference.para: Optional: a copy of the points with Visit_Order (1, 2, 3, ...), Src_FID (the source Object ID), and Leg_km (the length of the leg leaving each stop). Label by Visit_Order and the map reads like an itinerary.

param.displayname: Extra randomized solver attempts (more = sometimes slightly shorter routes, slower)

scriptExample.title: Estimated Shortest Path example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: A round trip through survey stations from the parking spot, with the visit-ordered points saved alongside the route.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # mode options (matching is by prefix): # "Simple Shortest Path" # "Start and End at Same Point" # "Start and End at Different Specified Points" result = arcpy.jenness.EstimatedShortestPath( in_points=r"D:\data\study.gdb\stations", mode="Start and End at Same Point", loop_point=r"D:\data\study.gdb\parking", out_route=r"D:\data\study.gdb\stations_Route", out_points=r"D:\data\study.gdb\stations_Visit_Order") print(result.getOutput(2)) # stops visited print(result.getOutput(3)) # route length, km

(1958), A method for solving traveling-salesman problems, Operations Research 6(6):791-812, https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.6.6.791, and Or-opt segment relocation as described by Babin, G., S. Deneault, and G. Laporte (2007), Improvements to the Or-opt heuristic for the symmetric travelling salesman problem, Journal of the Operational Research Society 58(3):402-407, https://doi.org/10.1057/palgrave.jors.2602160 (the move family is named for Ilhan Or's 1976 Northwestern dissertation, which we were unable to access). The variable-depth alternative discussed in the help: Lin, S., and B. W. Kernighan (1973), An effective heuristic algorithm for the traveling-salesman problem, Operations Research 21(2):498-516, https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.21.2.498.
